b: Our latest book, “America Obscura: An Explorer’s Guide to the Hidden Wonders of the United States,” has just been published. But it doesn’t just take you to Texas or Maine or Michigan. It takes you to a town called Hell, to a desert in one of the greenest states, to a sundial on the exact spot where America's day begins, and to a seven-story Jesus nicknamed “Our Milk Carton with Arms.”

These are real places you can visit, and they are so dang unique. Since you’ll be driving, riding the rails or flying to reach a lot of them, we built you a soundtrack to match. Every song here is tied to a specific spot in the book. The full playlist is below, but you can also stream it on Spotify.
Institute of Illegal Images, San Francisco: a Victorian house holding 33,000 sheets of framed LSD blotter art.
Original Stash Tribute Plaque, Estacada, Ore.: the spot in the woods where the world's first geocache, the "Stash," was hidden in 2000.
Goonie Trails, Astoria, Ore.: Goonies never say die in the town where the movie was filmed.
One Square Inch of Silence, Olympic National Park, Wash.: one of the quietest places in the country. Cage's piece is four and a half minutes of literal silence; Tori is the version with sound.
Twede's Cafe, North Bend, Wash.: the real Double R Diner from Twin Peaks. Order the cherry pie.
London Bridge, Lake Havasu City, Ariz.: it fell all the way to Arizona, with a voodoo doll sealed inside.
Airmail Arrow, Reno, Nev.: before GPS, airmail pilots followed giant concrete arrows across the desert.
Loretto Chapel, Santa Fe, N.M.: a "miraculous" spiral staircase built without a single nail.
National Museum of Nuclear Science & History, Albuquerque, N.M.: home of Atomic Annie, the cannon that fired the first and last nuclear artillery shell.
Jesus in Cowboy Boots, Paris, Texas: a cemetery statue that swapped sandals for boots.
Cadillac Ranch, Amarillo, Texas: ten Cadillacs buried nose-down in a field, and the inspiration for this song.
The Orange Show, Houston: a retired mail carrier's folk-art maze built from salvage, set to a Houston band.
Congress Bridge Bats, Austin: 1.5 million bats pour out from under the bridge on summer nights.
Sri Sri Radha Krishna Temple, Spanish Fork, Utah: a Hare Krishna temple, and home to Utah's giant festival of colors.
International Church of Cannabis, Denver: a technicolor former Lutheran church where the services are, well, elevated.
Pikes Peak Summit House, Colorado: the summit that inspired the poem, now home to North America's highest donut fryer.
Craters of the Moon, Arco, Idaho: lava fields so lunar that you can almost do the moonwalk.
I.B. Perrine Bridge, Twin Falls, Idaho: the one U.S. bridge where you can BASE jump without a permit, all year.
Sip 'n Dip Lounge, Great Falls, Mont.: a tiki bar where live mermaids swim past your barstool.
Hole-in-the-Wall Outlaw Hideout, Kaycee, Wyo.: where Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid hid out.
They Also Ran Gallery, Norton, Kan.: the only gallery devoted to people who lost the presidency.
The Big Well, Greensburg, Kan.: the largest hand-dug well in the country, in a town rebuilt after a tornado.
Old Lincoln Highway, Omaha–Elkhorn, Neb.: three miles of century-old red brick on America's first coast-to-coast road.
Happy Jack Chalk Mine, Scotia, Neb.: an underground chalk mine you can tour.
KVLY-TV Mast, Blanchard, N.D.: a 1,987-foot TV tower that was once the tallest structure on Earth.
National Weather Museum, Norman, Okla.: storm-chasing gear in the state the musical is named for.
Wichita Mountains Buffalo Herd, Okla.: 650 bison descended from a Bronx Zoo breeding program.
Hall of Records, Mount Rushmore, S.D.: America's backup drive, sealed in a vault behind Lincoln's head.
The Super Museum, Metropolis, Ill.: 70,000 items devoted to the Man of Steel, in a town actually named Metropolis.
City Methodist Church, Gary, Ind.: a nine-story Gothic ruin left behind by the steel industry's crash.
Iowa 80 Truck Stop, Walcott, Iowa: the world's largest truck stop, complete with barber, dentist and trucking museum.
Maharishi Vedic City, Iowa: a whole town built around Transcendental Meditation.
Hell, Michigan: for $100 you can be mayor for a day, and the job comes with horns.
Great Lakes Shipwreck Museum, Paradise, Mich.: where the Fitzgerald's bell is remembered.
The Big Fish Supper Club, Bena, Minn.: dinner beside a 65-foot muskie with very sharp teeth.
City Museum, St. Louis: a ten-story playground of slides, tunnels and salvage, in the city of the 1904 World's Fair.
Harry Andrews' Chateau Laroche, Loveland, Ohio: a full-scale medieval castle one man built by hand.
House on the Rock, Spring Green, Wis.: "an infinite-seeming collection of collections," with always another room.
Sputnik IV Crash Site, Manitowoc, Wis.: where a chunk of Soviet satellite landed in the street in 1962.
"Welcome to Cleveland" Sign, Milwaukee: a rooftop prank confusing airline passengers since 1978.
Sussex Tavern at Rabbit's Ferry House, Lewes, Del.: colonial cocktails in a re-created 1740 tavern in the first town of the first state.
Iron Hill School No. 112C, Newark, Del.: a one-room schoolhouse preserving Delaware's segregated past.
National Cryptologic Museum, Fort Meade, Md.: the codebreaking gadgets that decided history.
Madam Marie's Psychic Booth, Asbury Park, N.J.: the boardwalk fortune-teller Springsteen wrote into this song.
Site of the 1916 Shark Attacks, Matawan, N.J.: the attacks a mile up a creek that helped inspire Jaws.
George Washington's Distillery, Alexandria, Va.: the first president's whiskey side hustle.
The Mutilated Currency Division, Washington, D.C.: the federal office that refunds burned, chewed and laundered cash, even from inside a cow.
The Preamble in License Plates, Washington, D.C.: "We the People," spelled out in vanity plates.
New River Gorge Bridge, Fayetteville, W.Va.: once a year on Bridge Day, people jump off it on purpose.
Annual Burning of Benedict Arnold, New London, Conn.: the town still burns its hometown traitor in effigy.
The Desert of Maine, Freeport: 40 acres of sand in one of the greenest states.
The Wilhelm Reich Museum, Rangeley, Maine: the home of the man this song is literally about, rain-making machine included.
Wild Blueberry Land, Columbia Falls, Maine: a theme park for the state fruit.
Ponyhenge, Lincoln, Mass.: a mysterious, ever-growing herd of rocking horses in a field.
Mystery Hill: America's Stonehenge, Salem, N.H.: ancient site or wishful thinking? You decide.
Clark's Trading Post, Lincoln, N.H.: trained bears, a steam train, and the Wolfman, who chases it.
The First Shaker Village, Albany, N.Y.: the Shakers' first settlement, and the people who wrote this song.
"It's the End of the World as We Know It"
Cobb's Hill, Rochester, N.Y.: where believers waited for the world to end in 1844. It didn't.
Star Trek Original Series Set Tour, Ticonderoga, N.Y.: the Enterprise bridge, rebuilt in an old supermarket by an Elvis impersonator.
The Fantastic Umbrella Factory, Charlestown, R.I.: a 250-year-old farm turned hippie bazaar.
Carrie Furnaces, Pittsburgh: towering blast furnaces from Pennsylvania's steel age.
Lake Morey Skate Trail, Fairlee, Vt.: the longest outdoor skate trail in the U.S.
The Grave of Miss Baker, Huntsville, Ala.: America's first monkey to return alive from space. Bring a banana.
Billy Bass Adoption Center, Little Rock, Ark.: where singing animatronic fish go to retire.
Christ of the Ozarks, Eureka Springs, Ark.: a seven-story Jesus nicknamed "Our Milk Carton with Arms."
Trap Music Museum, Atlanta: T.I.'s museum, and the song the book says to play on the way there.
Gallop to Glory, Louisville, Ky.: a hidden walk of fame of Derby-winning jockeys' handprints.
LIGO Livingston Observatory, La.: the instrument that first caught gravitational waves.
Mardi Gras World, New Orleans: the factory where the floats are built.
Robert Johnson's Grave, Greenwood, Miss.: fans leave guitar picks for the man who made a deal at the crossroads.
Emmett Till Historic Intrepid Center, Glendora, Miss.: a museum keeping his story in the place it happened.
Woolworth Lunch Counter Sit-in, Greensboro, N.C.: where four students sat down on Feb. 1, 1960, and changed history.
The Mother Vine, Manteo, N.C.: perhaps the oldest grapevine in North America.
General Johnson & the Chairmen of the Board
Fat Harold's Beach Club, North Myrtle Beach, S.C.: the beating heart of the shag, South Carolina's state dance.
Tina Turner Museum, Brownsville, Tenn.: the one-room schoolhouse Tina attended as a kid in Nutbush.
Dolly Parton's Dream Box, Pigeon Forge, Tenn.: her last song, sealed until her 100th birthday in 2046.
The Fountain of Youth, St. Augustine, Fla.: take a sip. Results not guaranteed.
Weeki Wachee: City of Live Mermaids, Fla.: Florida had mermaids before Disney did.
Dry Tortugas, Fla.: a remote island fort 70 miles past Key West.
Turnagain Arm Bore Tide, Anchorage, Alaska: surfing a 10-foot tidal wave in a drysuit.
Pu'uhonua o Hōnaunau, Hawaii: an ancient place of refuge for anyone who broke a sacred law and made it here.
Lanai Cat Sanctuary, Hawaii: an island of 3,000 people and more than 500 cats.
Yokoi's Cave, Guam: the hideout of a Japanese soldier who didn't surrender until 1972.
El Batey, San Juan, P.R.: a graffiti-covered dive bar in Old San Juan.
Point Udall, St. Croix, U.S.V.I.: a giant sundial at the easternmost point of the U.S.
Point Udall, St. Croix, U.S.V.I.: where each day in the United States begins.
